title: Writing Is Thinking, Part I
author: Learning to Learn Well
summary: This is the first installment of a longer series arguing that writing is not merely a vehicle for communicating an already-finished thought, but one of the primary tools by which thinking itself gets done. The author develops three connected claims: writing is a symbolic act of meaning-making that never perfectly captures an inner experience; writing for an audience is a staged performance distinct from the private, exploratory writing that should precede it; and writing functions as a tool of understanding, not just communication, because a first draft reveals gaps, contradictions, and missing pieces that stayed invisible while an idea remained only a feeling in the mind. The piece leans on cognitive-science-adjacent sources — William Zinsser's Writing to Learn and Daniel Willingham's Outsmart Your Brain — to argue that writing-to-learn research supports explaining, connecting, and interpreting content as the mechanisms through which writing improves learning. The essay closes with a pointed argument about generative AI: AI did not invent passive learning, but it made polished-looking passivity far easier to produce, since a fluent AI-generated summary can look like understanding without requiring any of the retrieval or organizing work that actually builds it. The author's own position on AI use is nuanced rather than rejectionist — useful after a person has begun thinking, not as a substitute for the initial private drafting stage.
points: Distinguishes writing as private meaning-making (writing for yourself first) from writing as public performance (writing for an audience), arguing that collapsing the two too early — self-editing before ideas are explored — blocks genuine discovery.

Reframes the standard model of writing (thought first, writing second, communication third) by arguing that writing is frequently part of how a thought becomes understandable in the first place, not just its output.
Grounds the argument in writing-to-learn research and Willingham's cognitive science, tying the value of writing to retrieval, connection-making, and interpretation rather than transcription.

Makes a specific, non-alarmist case about AI: it did not create passive learning but made "polished-looking passivity" cheaper to produce, since fluent AI text can mimic the appearance of understanding without the underlying cognitive work.
Positions AI as most useful only after a person's own rough draft or notebook already exists, reversing the common workflow of asking AI to generate a starting point.
quotes: Most of the time I understand something because I can feel the general shape of the idea in my mind. But when I try to write it down, I discover that the idea is incomplete.
Writing is more than a way to communicate a finished thought. It's one of the best ways we discover what we think.
If you begin criticizing every sentence before you have given yourself a chance to explore the idea, you may prevent yourself from discovering what you actually think.

Writing is useful because it gives you a place for your thoughts to be sorted out, which makes it easier to visually organize them. Your first explanation isn't going to be perfect, but that's okay because it's only for your eyes anyway.
This matters even more in the age of artificial intelligence because AI did not create passive learning. It made polished-looking passivity easier to produce.
My notebook, rough draft, or unfinished explanation gives AI something meaningful to respond to.
Writing is not only what happens after thinking. Writing is one of the places where thinking happens.
